title: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
summary: Why a short question and the passage that answers it should be embedded in different roles, how models and APIs mark the role, what breaks when you mix roles up, and how to test it.
outcomes: Explain why short queries and long passages come from different distributions and why similar is not the same as relevant
Compare the ways systems mark the role: two encoders, role prefixes, task instructions and API input types
Compute, on a toy example, how using one input type on both sides flips the top result from answer to duplicate
Diagnose input-type bugs in indexing and query paths, including mixed indexes and symmetric tasks
Design a test grid of query and document settings scored with recall@k and nDCG@10 on your own data

lessons.title: Why a question is not a short version of its answer

blocks.md:
From the prerequisite course you know the **bi-encoder**: one encoder turns each text into a vector on its own, and search ranks passages by cosine similarity to the query vector. Contrastive training made cosine meaningful by pulling paired texts together.

This course is about a detail that bi-encoder hides. The encoder sees one string at a time, so unless you tell it, it cannot know whether that string is a **query** (something a user typed to find information) or a **document** (something stored in the index to be found).

The two sides of a search system are different kinds of text:

- **Length.** Queries are a few words or one question. Passages are paragraphs, often filled up to the model's input limit.
- **Form.** Queries are questions or keyword lists. Passages are declarative statements.
- **Content.** A query states a need and lacks the facts. A passage carries facts, most of which have nothing to do with any one query.
- **Relation.** A good passage *answers* the query. It does not *mean the same thing* as the query.

In statistical terms, queries and passages are samples from two different distributions of text, and relevance is a relation between the two, not similarity within one.

The Sentence Transformers docs name the two cases. In **symmetric** search, query and corpus entries have about the same length and content, such as finding "How to learn Python on the web?" for the query "How to learn Python online?". In **asymmetric** search, a short query such as "What is Python" should find a longer paragraph that answers it.

Their test is useful: in a symmetric task you could swap the query and the corpus entry and nothing would change. In an asymmetric task, flipping them usually makes no sense.

blocks.prompt: The Nomic Embed paper uses this example. Query: "What is the capital of France?" Candidate 1: "What is the name of the capital city of France?" Candidate 2: "Paris is the capital of France." Which candidate should be closer to the query?
blocks.reveal: It depends on the task, which is exactly the problem. The paper says a semantic similarity task would consider the first candidate closest, while a question answering task would consider the second closest. A model trained on both kinds of pairs without being told which task it is doing receives a **conflicting training signal**. Nomic's fix, like E5's, is a task prefix on every input, so the model can learn both behaviors and you pick one at inference.

blocks.title: Toy: cosine with the query "What is the capital of France?"

scenes.caption: One encoder, no roles (a hand-built toy, lesson 3 shows the math). The duplicate question D1 scores 0.99 because it matches the query's topic and its question form. The passage that answers it, D2, gets 0.57.
Same texts, but the query is encoded in query mode and the corpus in document mode. Now the answer D2 wins, 0.97 against 0.83. The topic still matters; the role decides which kind of match counts.

blocks.md: This is not a contrived corner case. Real corpora are full of question-shaped text: FAQ pages, forum thread titles, support tickets, quiz banks. The E5 authors report that their asymmetric design "turns out to be important for some retrieval tasks where there exist paraphrases of the query in the target corpus." A symmetric encoder ranks those paraphrases above the passage that holds the answer, because surface form is part of what it learned to match.

Misconception: *a text's embedding is a fixed property of the text.* In a role-aware model the same string gets one vector as a query and a different vector as a document, by design. Which vector you get depends on how you called the model.
Search is asymmetric. Queries and documents differ in length, form and role, and relevance means *answers*, not *looks like*. Tell the model which side each text is on.

blocks.question: Which of these is a symmetric task in the Sentence Transformers sense?
options: Retrieving help-center paragraphs for a user's question in a RAG app
Finding forum questions that duplicate a newly posted question
Matching a two-word product search to full product descriptions
Finding code snippets that implement a natural-language request
blocks.explain: Duplicate detection compares texts of the same kind: you could swap the new question and the stored one and the task would not change. The other three pair a short need with a longer text that satisfies it, so flipping them makes no sense.

blocks.question: Your corpus is a support site where every article starts with the question it answers, followed by the answer. Why does that make role-aware encoding more important, not less?
options: Long articles get truncated, so the role is lost
Role prefixes only work on corpora without questions
Question-shaped text in the corpus is exactly where a symmetric encoder prefers paraphrases over answers
Cosine similarity cannot compare questions with articles
blocks.explain: E5 found the asymmetric design matters most when the corpus contains paraphrases of the query. Here every article opens with one, so form-matching can pull in articles that merely ask a similar question, and the role signal is what makes answer content count.

lessons.title: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on

blocks.md: There are two ways to make an encoder role-aware: give each role its own weights, or keep one set of weights and mark the role in the input. Products and libraries wrap these in a few different interfaces. This lesson walks through each, from the original research to the API parameter you set today.

blocks.caption: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR): a question encoder E_Q and a passage encoder E_P, scored by dot product. Karpukhin et al. used two independent BERT-base networks and took the [CLS] output, d = 768.

blocks.md:
**1. Two encoders (DPR).** Karpukhin et al. (2020) trained a question encoder and a passage encoder as two independent BERT networks. Each side can specialize: one learns to read short questions, the other long passages. The cost is two sets of weights, and the training objective only ever compared a question vector with a passage vector. On open-domain QA, this dual encoder beat a strong Lucene BM25 system by 9 to 19 points absolute in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy.

**2. One encoder, a role prefix (E5, Nomic Embed).** E5 "use[s] a shared encoder for all input texts and break[s] the symmetry by adding two prefix identifiers": every query starts with `query: ` and every passage with `passage: `. For pairs where neither side is clearly the query, such as citation pairs, they picked one at random. Nomic Embed uses `search_query: ` and `search_document: ` the same way.

blocks.title: Where the role enters the model

scenes.caption: DPR: two separate networks. The role is baked into the weights, so the query never touches the passage encoder.
E5 and Nomic: one shared encoder. A literal text prefix marks the role, so the encoder sees different tokens and produces a different vector for the same sentence.
INSTRUCTOR: the marker is a full task instruction naming the text type, domain and goal. Asymmetric tasks get two different instructions; symmetric tasks use the same one on both sides.

labels.preQ:
Represent the Wikipedia
question for retrieving
labels.preD:
Represent the Wikipedia
document for retrieval:

scenes.caption: BGE: an instruction on the query side only. Passages go in as plain text. Adding the instruction to passages would be the bug here.
Hosted APIs: you pass a parameter and the provider applies the role inside its service. Voyage documents that it prepends a prompt; for other providers the mechanism is not public.

blocks.md:
**3. Task instructions (INSTRUCTOR, BGE).** INSTRUCTOR (Su et al.) embeds every text together with an instruction describing the task and domain, for example "Represent the Wikipedia question for retrieving supporting documents: " on queries and "Represent the Wikipedia document for retrieval: " on documents. The authors wrote instructions for 330 training tasks. For symmetric tasks the two sides get the same instruction; for asymmetric ones they differ.

BGE (from the C-Pack paper) attaches an instruction to the **query side only**. Its English v1.5 model card gives "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: " for short-query-to-passage retrieval and says that no instruction needs to be added to passages. That card also calls the instruction optional for v1.5, reporting only "a slight degradation in retrieval performance" without it.

**4. API parameters.** Hosted embedding APIs expose the role as a field:

- **Cohere** `input_type`: `search_document` for texts stored in a vector database, `search_query` for queries run against it, plus `classification`, `clustering` and `image`. The API reference marks it required for v3 and later embedding models.
- **Voyage** `input_type`: `None` (default), `query` or `document`. The docs say it prepends "Represent the query for retrieving supporting documents: " or "Represent the document for retrieval: ".
- **Gemini API** `task_type`: `RETRIEVAL_QUERY` and `RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT`, plus `SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY`, `CLASSIFICATION`, `CLUSTERING` and query-side variants (`QUESTION_ANSWERING`, `FACT_VERIFICATION`, `CODE_RETRIEVAL_QUERY`) that pair with `RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT` on the corpus.

These interfaces change between model generations: the Gemini docs say a newer model does not accept `task_type` and wants the task written into the text instead. Check the docs for the exact model you use.

blocks.code:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

# Prompts can come from the model's saved config, or be given here.
model = SentenceTransformer(MODEL_ID,
    prompts={"query": "query: ", "document": "passage: "})

q = model.encode_query(["how do I reset my password"])
d = model.encode_document(["To reset your password, open Settings, then Security."])
print(model.similarity(q, d))
blocks.caption: Sentence Transformers: encode_query applies the "query" prompt; encode_document applies the first of "document", "passage" or "corpus". MODEL_ID is a placeholder: use the prompts its model card specifies.

blocks.md: In Sentence Transformers, `encode_query` and `encode_document` differ from plain `encode` in two ways: they pick the saved query or document prompt, and they set the task to query or document. A **Router** module uses that task to send each side through different submodules, which covers the DPR case too, for example a cheap static embedding for queries and a transformer for documents. The docs add a warning worth remembering: if a model has no saved prompts or task routes, all three methods return **identical** embeddings.

Prefixes are literal strings, trailing space included. Copy them from the model card exactly; a near miss such as `Query:` instead of `query: ` is a different input from the one the model was trained on.
All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

blocks.question: You use a BGE-style model whose card says to prepend an instruction to short queries. A teammate prepends the same instruction to every passage at indexing time "for consistency". What is wrong?
options: Nothing; using the same instruction on both sides is how asymmetric models are meant to work
The model was trained with the instruction on queries only, so passages now look like queries and lose their document representation
Instructions are ignored at indexing time, so it only wastes tokens
It makes cosine scores negative
blocks.explain: BGE attaches the instruction to the query side only, and its card says no instruction is added to passages. Instructed passages are encoded as if they were queries, which is the "everything as query" mismatch you will see in the toy next lesson.

blocks.question: You call encode_query and encode_document on a model and get exactly the same vectors for the same text. What is the most likely explanation?
options: encode_query always normalizes and encode_document never does
The model is a DPR-style dual encoder
The vectors are cached from the first call
The model has no saved query or document prompts or routes, so both calls fall back to plain encode
blocks.explain: The Sentence Transformers docs say that if a model was not trained with predefined prompts or task types, encode, encode_query and encode_document return identical embeddings. Either the model is genuinely symmetric, or you need to pass the prompts from its model card yourself.

lessons.title: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result

blocks.md:
Now build the effect from scratch with numbers you can check. This is a **hand-built toy**, simplified to 4 dimensions so each one has a meaning. Real models learn these behaviors spread across hundreds of dimensions, but the arithmetic is the same: encode, normalize, take dot products.

Each text gets four raw features: about France ($f$), about Germany ($g$), question form ($s$), and contains an answer, here a named capital city ($a$).

The texts and their raw features $[f, g, s, a]$:

- **Q1** "What is the capital of France?" $[0.8, 0, 0.6, 0]$
- **Q2** "Which city is Germany's capital?" $[0, 0.8, 0.6, 0]$
- **D1** "What is the name of the capital city of France?" $[0.7, 0, 0.7, 0]$
- **D2** "Paris is the capital and largest city of France." $[0.7, 0, 0, 0.7]$
- **D3** "What is the name of the capital city of Germany?" $[0, 0.7, 0.7, 0]$
- **D4** "Berlin is the capital of Germany." $[0, 0.7, 0, 0.7]$

D1 and D3 are the FAQ-style paraphrases; D2 and D4 are the answers. The correct result for Q1 is D2 and for Q2 is D4.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} v_{\text{none}} &= \mathrm{norm}([f,\ g,\ s,\ a]) \\ v_{\text{query}} &= \mathrm{norm}([f,\ g,\ 0.2s,\ 0.9s]) \\ v_{\text{doc}} &= \mathrm{norm}([f,\ g,\ 0.2s,\ a]) \end{aligned}
blocks.caption: Three toy encoding modes. Query mode turns "this is a question" into "a good match contains an answer". Document mode keeps the answer feature. Both shrink the surface form. norm scales to unit length.

blocks.md:
Read the modes as what role training teaches. Without roles, form counts fully, so questions match questions. In **query mode** the model learns that a question predicts its answer's content: question form is written into the answer slot. In **document mode** the model records whether the text contains answer content. Cosine of two unit vectors is just their dot product.

Check one by hand. In query mode Q1 becomes $[0.8, 0, 0.12, 0.54]$, length 0.973, so $[0.823, 0, 0.123, 0.555]$. In document mode D2 is $[0.707, 0, 0, 0.707]$. Dot product: $0.823 \times 0.707 + 0.555 \times 0.707 = 0.974$.

blocks.prompt: Suppose a single helper embeds everything in **document** mode, queries included. Using the formulas above, which document comes out on top for Q1, and roughly by how much?
blocks.reveal: **D1, the duplicate question**, at 0.999 against 0.699 for the answer D2. In document mode Q1 becomes $[0.989, 0, 0.148, 0]$: almost pure France, with no answer feature, because only query mode turns question form into answer expectation. D1 in document mode is also almost pure France, so they align. D2's answer feature is weight the query vector cannot match, which costs it 0.3.

blocks.title: Toy cosines: rows are queries, columns are documents

scenes.caption: No roles: both sides encoded the same plain way. Each query's top hit (highlighted) is its duplicate question at 0.99; the answers get 0.57.
Everything in document mode. Duplicates win harder: 1.00 against 0.70. The queries carry no answer expectation, so the answers' strongest feature goes unmatched.
Everything in query mode. Documents encoded as queries: the duplicates gain the answer-expectation feature too (0.99), and the true answers lose their answer feature (0.82). Duplicates still win.
Correct roles: queries in query mode, documents in document mode. The answers win, 0.97 against 0.83 for the duplicates. Recall@1 (queries whose top hit is the answer) goes from 0 of 2 to 2 of 2.

blocks.md:
Three lessons hide in that matrix.

1. **Same type on both sides fails in every variant.** No roles, all document, all query: each one matches like with like, and the duplicate wins.
2. **Roles reweight; they do not erase topic.** Under correct roles D1 still scores 0.83, because it really is about France's capital. The margin that flips the ranking is 0.14.
3. **Role features can leak across topics.** Q1 scores 0.39 against D4, the Berlin answer, because "expects an answer" matches "contains an answer" regardless of country. Real models have far more topic dimensions, but this is why an off-topic passage that is shaped like an answer can sneak into the candidates.

blocks.code:
import math
F = {"Q1": [0.8, 0, 0.6, 0], "D1": [0.7, 0, 0.7, 0], "D2": [0.7, 0, 0, 0.7]}

def enc(t, mode):
    f, g, s, a = F[t]
    v = {"none": [f, g, s, a],
         "query": [f, g, 0.2 * s, 0.9 * s],
         "document": [f, g, 0.2 * s, a]}[mode]
    n = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in v))
    return [x / n for x in v]

cos = lambda u, v: sum(x * y for x, y in zip(u, v))
for qm, dm in [("none", "none"), ("query", "document")]:
    print(qm, dm, [round(cos(enc("Q1", qm), enc(d, dm)), 3) for d in ("D1", "D2")])
# none none [0.99, 0.566]
# query document [0.831, 0.974]
blocks.caption: The script behind the figures, trimmed to Q1, D1 and D2. Every number in this lesson came from it.

blocks.md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

blocks.question: In the toy, which configuration does a codebase have if one embed() helper hard-codes the query input type and is used both to build the index and to search it?
options: Everything in query mode
No roles
Everything in document mode
Correct roles
blocks.explain: Both sides go through query mode, so the stored documents are encoded as if they were queries. In the toy that ranks the duplicate questions first (0.99) and drops the answers to 0.82.

blocks.question: Under correct roles, why does the duplicate question D1 still score 0.83 with Q1?
options: Because query mode is applied to D1 by mistake
Because cosine similarity of any two questions is at least 0.8
Because the role changes how form and answer content are weighted but the shared France topic still aligns the vectors
Because D1 is longer than Q1
blocks.explain: Role encoding reweights features; it does not remove topic. D1 really is about the capital of France, so it stays a strong candidate. What changes is that the answer passage now scores higher, by a margin of 0.14 in this toy.

blocks.md: In a real system, indexing and querying are separate code paths, often written months apart. The input type is set in each one, and **nothing fails if they disagree**: the vectors have the same dimension, the index accepts them, and search returns plausible neighbors. The only symptom is worse ranking, which nobody notices without an evaluation set. That makes input-type bugs silent quality bugs.

blocks.title: Two embedding call sites, one shared index

scenes.caption: Correct: the indexing path uses the document type, the query path uses the query type, both with the same model.
Bug: a shared helper defaults to the query type and the indexer never overrides it. Every stored vector is a query-mode vector, so question-shaped chunks win.
Bug: a prefix model (E5 style) where the query path sends raw text. The E5 card says to expect degraded performance without the prefixes.
Bug: a partial backfill. Old vectors were embedded without an input type, new ones with it. Two populations now compete in one ranking, and one may score systematically higher.
Bug: the model was upgraded on the query path only. Vectors from different models are not comparable even at the same dimension; the Gemini docs say re-embed when upgrading.

blocks.caption: A pattern that ships the bug in scene 2. The client call is illustrative, not a specific SDK.

blocks.question: What is the bug in the code above, and what is the smallest correct fix?
options: search() should pass input_type="search_document"
embed() should be called once per text instead of in a batch
There is no bug, because the same model is used on both paths
index_chunks() relies on the query default; pass input_type="search_document" there, and better, remove the default so every call site must choose
blocks.explain: The indexer silently inherits the query type, so the whole corpus is stored as queries. Passing the document type fixes it; removing the default turns the next forgotten argument into an immediate error instead of a silent ranking loss.

blocks.md:
**Symmetric tasks need the same type on both sides.** When both texts play the same role, giving them different roles is the mistake:

- E5's card says to use `query: ` for symmetric tasks such as semantic similarity and paraphrase retrieval, and also when using embeddings as features. For BEIR's Quora duplicate task the paper put `query: ` on every question.
- Nomic uses one prefix on both sides for symmetric tasks: `classification` for STS-style rephrasals, `clustering` for grouping.
- INSTRUCTOR uses the same instruction on both sides of a symmetric task.
- Cohere offers `classification` and `clustering`; the Gemini API offers `SEMANTIC_SIMILARITY`, `CLASSIFICATION` and `CLUSTERING`.

So the right question is not "query or document?" but "what role does this text play in this task?". The same FAQ entry can be a document in RAG and a query-side text in duplicate detection.

**Mixing is a per-provider question.** Voyage's docs state that embeddings made with and without `input_type` are compatible. That is a guarantee about Voyage's models, not a general law. For open models trained with prefixes, treat each combination of model and input type as its own vector format: do not mix formats in one index unless you have measured that it is safe.

**Prefixes cost input length.** A prefix or instruction is ordinary text, so it uses part of the model's maximum input. Long instructions on long passages push content past the truncation point; chunk with the prefix included in the token count.

Record the model id and the input type (or exact prefix string) alongside the index, and check them at query time. When either changes, build a new index and switch over, rather than re-embedding part of the old one in place.

blocks.question: You want to cluster 50,000 support tickets by topic with an API that offers search_query, search_document, classification and clustering types. Which setup matches the docs?
options: search_query for half the tickets and search_document for the other half
The clustering type for every ticket
search_document for all tickets, since they are stored documents
No input type, because clustering does not use cosine
blocks.explain: Clustering compares tickets with each other, a symmetric task, so every text gets the same role. Cohere documents a clustering type for exactly this, and Nomic uses a clustering prefix on both sides. Splitting the tickets across query and document types would make the halves systematically different.

blocks.question: After a partial backfill, half your index was embedded with the document type and half without any type, on a prefix-trained open model. What symptom should you look for first?
options: Results skew toward one population: one half ranks systematically higher regardless of relevance
Queries fail with a dimension mismatch error
Search latency doubles
Nothing; the two halves are interchangeable for all models
blocks.explain: Both halves have the same dimension, so nothing errors. But they are different vector formats, so cosine scores against a query are not on the same footing. Check what fraction of top results comes from each half compared with its share of the corpus.

lessons.title: Testing input types on your own data

blocks.md:
Published numbers tell you the average effect, which is often modest. In the C-Pack ablation (Table 3, evaluated on the Chinese benchmark C-MTEB), removing the query instruction from BGE fine-tuning lowered the retrieval score from 71.53 to 70.55. The Sentence Transformers prompt-training guide reports relative nDCG@10 gains under 1% from training with prompts in its runs.

Averages hide what matters to you: how many of *your* queries flip, and whether your corpus has the question-shaped documents where symmetric encoding fails. And mismatches (indexing as queries, mixed indexes) have no published bound. So measure on your own data.

blocks.title: C-Pack ablation: with vs without the query instruction (C-MTEB)

scenes.caption: Retrieval average on C-MTEB: 71.53 with the instruction, 70.55 without it. A real but small average gain.
STS in the same table: 54.98 with, 53.00 without. Not every category gains: clustering scored 50.01 without and 48.39 with. These are averages; individual queries can still flip.

blocks.md:
A test plan that catches both the modest average effect and the silent bugs:

1. **Build a labeled set.** Real queries from logs, each with the documents that answer it. Include question-shaped documents (FAQ titles, forum posts) if your corpus has them, since E5 found that is where the asymmetric design matters.
2. **Embed the corpus once per document-side setting** you want to compare, and the queries once per query-side setting.
3. **Run the grid.** At least (query, document), (document, document), (query, query) and (none, none). Score each with recall@k (share of a query's relevant documents in the top k) and nDCG@10 (0 to 1, also rewards ranking relevant documents higher in the top 10). nDCG@10 is the main retrieval metric in MTEB, which reuses BEIR's datasets and evaluation.
4. **Read the flips.** For queries whose top result changed between settings, look at both results. That is where you learn what the role is doing on your data.
5. **Compare like with like.** When you check a model against its published benchmark score, use the prefixes its authors used in evaluation.

blocks.title: A tiny input-type test on the toy corpus

scenes.caption: The sanity check runs first. The same text in query mode and document mode has cosine 0.832, so the role really changes the vector. A value of exactly 1 would mean the wrapper drops the parameter or the model has no roles.
Correct roles, first query. Scores for Q1: D1 0.831, D2 0.974, D3 0.024, D4 0.393. The top is D2, the gold answer.
Q2 also hits its answer D4 (0.974 against 0.831 for D3). Recall@1 is 2 of 2.
Both sides in document mode: Q1 picks D1 (0.999) and Q2 picks D3. Recall@1 drops to 0.
Both sides in query mode: duplicates win again (0.99 against 0.82). The grid makes the bug visible in one line of output each.

blocks.md:
Turn the sanity check into permanent tests, because input-type bugs come back with every refactor:

- **Role is applied:** cosine between query-mode and document-mode embeddings of the same text is below 1 for a model that has roles.
- **Call sites are right:** in unit tests, mock the embedding client and assert the indexer passes the document type and the search path passes the query type.
- **Index metadata matches:** the model id and input type stored with the index equal what the query path is about to use.
- **Regression gate:** rerun the labeled-set recall after any change to the embedding code, model or prompts.

Never assume the input type is right because results look plausible. Measure the grid of query and document settings on your own labeled queries, and keep tests that fail loudly when a call site or the index metadata drifts.

blocks.question: Your sanity check prints a cosine of exactly 1.000 between the query-mode and document-mode embeddings of the same sentence. What should you conclude?
options: Roles are working perfectly
The two modes are compatible, so you can mix them freely
The role is not being applied: the wrapper drops the parameter, or the model has no prompts or routes, so check the model card and pass its prefixes
Cosine similarity is broken for normalized vectors
blocks.explain: Role-aware encoding should give a different vector per role. Identical vectors mean the role never reached the model. Sentence Transformers returns identical embeddings from encode_query and encode_document when the model has no saved prompts or routes.

blocks.question: On your labeled set, (document, document) scores the same recall@10 as (query, document). What is the best next step?
options: Switch to (document, document) everywhere because it is simpler
Keep the documented pairing, check whether your set includes question-shaped documents and hard cases, and compare per-query flips and nDCG@10 before deciding
Conclude that the model is symmetric
Drop recall and use only cosine thresholds
blocks.explain: A tie on one metric over one set is weak evidence. The failure shows up when the corpus contains paraphrases of queries, and recall@10 can hide reordering inside the top 10. The documented pairing is what the model was trained with, so departing from it needs a measured reason.
